Back 4 Blood is visually great and the gunplay feels modern. But the problem is, it doesn’t understand what made Left 4 Dead 2 unforgettable.

Left 4 Dead 2 is simple yet satisfying. Just pick a gun, survive the chaos, work together, move to the safe room.

Back 4 Blood added too many systems that made the experience feel like a chore. Cards, builds, supply points, grinding. And instead of focusing on pure teamwork and unpredictable panic moments, they turned it into a meta progression shooter.

The zombies also don’t feel as iconic or scary as the Special Infected we faced in Left 4 Dead 2. The AI Director in Back 4 Blood often feels scripted, while Left 4 Dead 2’s chaos felt natural and unexpected.

Many Left 4 Dead 2 players wanted a modern spiritual sequel, but what we got felt like a live service game forced to be “more complicated” than it needed to be.

In the end, Back 4 Blood is not a BAD game, but it never captured the soul and simplicity that made Left 4 Dead 2 legendary, which is why a lot of Left 4 Dead 2 players hated it and went back to the classic.

If you’re a big Left 4 Dead 2 fan, you might miss the classic feel, but Back 4 Blood is still worth trying if you want a fresh take on co-op zombie action. Just don’t expect it to be exactly like Left 4 Dead 2. It’s different, but still fun in its own way.

Back 4 Blood was marketed like the glorious spiritual successor to Left 4 Dead, but playing it feels like discovering someone tried to recreate a legendary meal using corporate PowerPoint presentations and energy drinks.

The entire game exists under the shadow of Left 4 Dead.
And the worst part?
It never escapes it for even a second.

Every trailer screamed:
“FROM THE CREATORS OF LEFT 4 DEAD.”

Which immediately set expectations at:
“Okay, this should be incredible.”

Then players launched the game and realized:
oh no…
this is what happens when you technically recreate the formula but completely miss the soul.

The combat LOOKS chaotic and exciting at first:

* zombies everywhere
* teammates yelling
* special infected attacking
* explosions
* panic moments

But after a while it starts feeling weirdly artificial, like the game is desperately trying to manufacture intensity instead of naturally creating it.

Left 4 Dead had simplicity that worked perfectly.
Back 4 Blood looked at that simplicity and said:
“What if we added 47 systems nobody asked for?”

Cards.
Builds.
Currencies.
Supply lines.
Rarities.
Attachments.
Stats.
Modifiers.
Deck optimization.

Bro I came here to shoot zombies, not create a spreadsheet build for “+7% reload speed while crouching near emotional support teammates.”

The card system is probably the biggest example.
Some people love it.
Others feel like it turns every run into:
“meta build optimization simulator.”

Instead of:
“survive with friends against impossible odds.”

And the special infected somehow manage to be both over-designed and less memorable at the same time.

Ask almost anyone about Left 4 Dead and they instantly remember:

* Tank
* Witch
* Hunter
* Smoker

Those enemies had personality.

Meanwhile Back 4 Blood special infected sound like rejected gym supplements:

* Crusher
* Bruiser
* Tallboy
* Exploder
* Reeker

Half of them look like swollen meat accidents sprinting toward you in slightly different ways.

And the balance at launch was brutal in the wrong kind of way.
Not:
“challenging.”
More like:
“the AI director personally hates your bloodline.”

Players would open a door and instantly get:

* swarmed
* webbed
* exploded
* pinned
* slammed into a wall
* set on fire
* emotionally destroyed

all before reloading once.

The gunplay itself is decent…
but somehow the teamwork never hits the same emotional highs as Left 4 Dead.

Back 4 Blood feels like a game where four people are individually shooting things near each other.

Left 4 Dead felt like four survivors desperately trying to stay alive together.

That difference is hard to explain technically, but you feel it immediately.

The characters also suffer from “Marvel dialogue syndrome.”
Everyone constantly talks like they’re auditioning for quirky apocalypse TikTok compilations.

Nobody shuts up.
Nobody sounds exhausted enough.
And almost none of the dialogue becomes iconic.

Meanwhile Left 4 Dead characters could say one sentence and instantly feel memorable:

* “Pills here!”
* “Boomer!”
* “Witch!”
* “Tank!”

Simple.
Clear.
Perfect.

Back 4 Blood overcomplicates everything while somehow feeling less impactful.

And the pacing is exhausting.
The game constantly throws:

* mutations
* hordes
* corruption cards
* bosses
* environmental hazards

at you nonstop like it’s terrified players might become bored if there’s 4 seconds of breathing room.

Ironically this makes the chaos feel LESS special.

If everything is intense all the time…
nothing is.

And the community reaction perfectly captured the problem:
people didn’t necessarily think Back 4 Blood was terrible.

They just kept thinking:
“Why would I play this instead of Left 4 Dead 2?”

Which is an absolutely devastating comparison to lose.

The saddest part is that the game clearly has effort behind it.
The graphics are better.
The customization is deeper.
The systems are more modern.

But somehow the overall experience feels colder and more manufactured.

Like a game assembled by committee after analyzing engagement metrics instead of understanding why people loved cooperative zombie games in the first place.

Back 4 Blood isn’t a horrible game.

It’s almost worse than that.

It’s a game that constantly reminds you of a better game while never becoming memorable enough to replace it.
Once you stop wishing this had been LFD3 and enjoy it for what it is, it's a lot of fun with friends.

I’m gonna be honest: if this game wasn’t constantly marketed as the “spiritual successor” to Left 4 Dead, I probably would’ve been much less harsh on it.

But that’s exactly the problem.

You CANNOT spend years telling people that Back 4 Blood is the successor to Left 4 Dead and that it’s made by the creators of Left 4 Dead, then deliver something that completely misses what made those games special in the first place.

Is it a terrible game?
No.

Is it Left 4 Dead 3?
Absolutely not.

The story is okay. The Cleaners are decent enough, the weapons feel good, and there are moments where you can see some genuinely cool ideas buried under everything else.

But man… the vibe just isn’t there.

Left 4 Dead 1 and 2 had this unique atmosphere that made every campaign memorable. The music, the characters, the pacing, the special infected, the simplicity of jumping in with friends and immediately having fun.

Back 4 Blood feels like it looked at Left 4 Dead and said:

“What if we added 37 systems, 12 currencies, card decks, progression trees and a bunch of DLCs?”

Instead of improving the formula, it feels like it overcomplicated it.

And speaking of DLCs…

There are WAY too many paid expansions for a game that never convinced me it deserved them in the first place.

Every time I played, I couldn’t stop comparing it to Left 4 Dead 2, and every single time it made me want to go play Left 4 Dead 2 instead.

That’s probably the biggest criticism I can give.

Not because Back 4 Blood is awful.

But because after a few hours I realized I’d rather replay a 2009 game than continue playing the supposed successor released more than a decade later.

Overall:

Good guns.
Decent story.
Some fun moments.

But as a “spiritual successor” to Left 4 Dead?

Massive disappointment.

It’s not a bad game.

It’s just painfully average living in the shadow of two masterpieces.

- The game is way too luck based, certain combinations of mutations are just "♥♥♥♥ you, lose now" even with the most optimal builds and some combinations just outright end your run if you don't have the right builds
- The AI, while better than launch, still sucks. They get distracted easy and you have to learn how to abuse the AI in obtuse ways (even more obtuse in not full squads). They are also genuinely useless for missions that require carrying items as they can't carry them
- A ton of missions have infinite hordes so bad that they're near impossible to win without a certain amount of firecrackers/pipe bombs
- A ton of cards were nerfed and never buffed so a ton of them just suck now and they abandoned the game so there's no hope of them ever buffing what they nerfed

[h1]Dogsh*t or a gem?[/h1]
[b]Here are 4 reasons not to buy/play Back 4 Blood:[/b]

1. The game won't receive any new updates. The developers posted a "goodbye" statement on Feb 2nd, 2023, in which they wrote that their work on B4B had come to an end and they had moved on to the next project.

2. Multiplayer is almost dead. Even if you can find a few occasional campaign partners, other game modes are completely dead.

3. Questionable design choices:

- No key mapping for the flashlight.
- No server list for multiplayer.
- The multiplayer and singleplayer experiences differ drastically. Playing the game in singleplayer is so much easier that it eliminates the need to play it in multiplayer and team up with other players, even for the hardest difficulty.

4. Performance is not great. The game usually runs smoothly, but sometimes, closer to the end of a level, I was getting ungodly frame drops out of nowhere, which could end my No Hope run in seconds. If you have a high-end PC, however, you have nothing to worry about.


[b]If you're still here :D, here are the reasons why I leave a positive review:[/b]

1. I believe the amount of hate this game received is undeserved. Marketing Back 4 Blood as a Left 4 Dead successor did it no favors, as it attracted thousands of Left 4 Dead supremacist hyenas that started mauling and gnawing B4B for everything that makes it different from Left 4 Dead.

2. I fell in love with the gameplay. It is dynamic, fast-paced, and sometimes unforgiving, but ultimately, extremely fun. If you don't expect it to be Left 4 Dead and just want a fun zombie shooter, you won't be disappointed.

3. I consider the card system to be a nice addition. You don't see this mechanic often in shooters, but in B4B, it is well done and adds an additional layer of complexity.

4. The game looks amazing. Even on medium graphics settings, the game looks pretty. On high-end PCs, the visual aspect is incredible.

As someone who lived and breathed Left 4 Dead 1 and 2, Back 4 Blood broke my heart. I was there through the hype, the developer updates, the promises of “spiritual successor” glory, and what we got instead feels like a game that completely misunderstood what made Left 4 Dead magic in the first place.

The card system is the worst kind of gimmick. It’s convoluted, unnecessary, and somehow manages to make every run feel less fun. Instead of clean, skill-based progression, you’re buried in deck-building menus that have no place in a game about shooting zombies with your friends. Nobody ever asked for Slay the Spire: Undead Edition. 
(Well actually, that sounds sick, BUT THAT'S BESIDES THE POINT.  IT DOESN'T WORK FOR THIS GAME.)

The gunplay feels clunky, movement is stiff, and the special zombies, sorry, [i] “Ridden” [/i] lack personality and impact. Even the AI Director, once a genius system that made every Left 4 Dead match feel alive, is now an unbalanced mess that can’t decide if it wants to be too easy or unfairly punishing. The atmosphere, pacing, and flow are all off, like a cover band playing the right notes but missing the soul.

And where’s the mod support? The versus mode? The charm? Gone. All sacrificed in favor of bloated systems and “live service” nonsense that nobody wanted. It’s painfully clear the devs were chasing trends instead of trusting the simple, perfect formula they helped create.

As a longtime fan and early supporter, this one stings. I wanted Back 4 Blood to be Left 4 Dead 3 in spirit. What we got was Left 4 Dead stripped of everything that made it timeless, replaced with a pile of half-baked ideas and soulless systems.

Verdict:
A tragic case of overthinking greatness. Back 4 Blood had the pedigree, the potential, and the fanbase, and wasted all three. 4/10.

Talking about this game always brings up the same unavoidable comparison: Left 4 Dead. But there is more to that! Back 4 Blood feels like the natural next step for people who love the Left 4 Dead formula but want more depth, character development and teamwork. It keeps that classic “4 survivors vs zombie horde” energy, but adds way more reasons to replay.

Both games are about blasting through infested maps and Back 4 Blood doesn’t change that core loop, it just layers more mechanics on top. Runs feel less basic and more tailored to you. Where Left 4 Dead is straightforward, this game gives you the tools to tinker, experiment and create builds for surviving the apocalypse. 

And here kicks in the big game changer - the card system. You build a deck that can boost things like stamina, ammo, healing, melee, team buffs and more. For example one player can lean into melee tank builds, another into healing and support, the third into damage etc. So the whole team feels actually like a proper co‑op squad instead of four clones.

Don't get me wrong, Left 4 Dead is great for "pick up and play", but Back 4 Blood makes teammates actually depend on each other. Higher difficulties really punish lone‑wolf behavior, so planning builds together and talking through strategies makes a huge difference. Because of the card system, runs feel fresher over time. You can replay the same map with a completely different setup and it plays out in new ways. As for me, Back 4 Blood has more reasons to come back than Left 4 Dead’s more static setup.

But to be fair, sometimes you just want it simple and Left 4 Dead wins here. You hop in, grab a gun, and go. With no decks to build or roles to think about. Its atmosphere and pacing are also super tight. Some people will always prefer that horror‑movie feeling over the slightly cartoony vibe.

This game isn’t trying and wouldn't be able to replace all the memories I have with Left 4 Dead. But it's the better pick, when I want to enjoy a co‑op shooter with builds and team roles but also want to keep the frantic and chaotic moments. For me Left 4 Dead is the timeless classic but Back 4 Blood is the upgraded version that finally lets me play that zombie apocalypse the way I want.

Well, I'm giving this a thumbs up because I enjoyed it for a while, and only considering that I paid about 2,99 for a key, plus 3,99 for the Annual Pass on Steam.

The game does a lot of things right, but there are also things that aren’t really enjoyable. 
Gameplay wise, it’s somehwat similar to L4D/L4D2, World War Z, Zombie Army 4, etc.

What I enjoyed about it were the level design, the graphics, some of the characters, the customization options, and the fact that the maps are long enough to fulfill my old Left 4 Dead needs.

Characters and zombie variations are not very creative, but they’re alright.

I had about 20 hours of fun with it before I lost interest for several reasons. 
With a more active player base, I might have played more, but ~5 years after release, I may be a bit late to the party.

What I don’t like are some of the gameplay choices.

Instead of making it a smooth “just play and enjoy” style like the aforementioned L4D or L4D2, they added an annoying perk card system that tries to add some variation. In practice, tho, it just annoys me and feels out of place in this game.

When you finish an Act, you get thrown back to Fort Hope, aka your “base camp,” so you lose the lobby and have to invite people again. This is especially annoying because it takes ages to find enough players in a public match to fill the lobby.

That’s another point. 
First of all, server connections take longer than I’d like, and then you’re mostly on your own with bots. 
If you're lucky enough, you'll have three friends to play with right now, otherwise, you might end up waiting 10+ minutes for other random people to join.

I didn’t mind playing with bots alone and it’s entirely possible to complete the game with bots on Recruit or Veteran. 

But is it fun?
Well, the first time through, when everything is new, yes. 
But the second time, I really would have preferred to play with other people.

So you wait and wait and wait. 
Then you finally get a full team, and I always had the issue that one person went AFK after one section. 

You can’t directly kick this person either. Why? Who knows. 
They will eventually be auto kicked after a while, but that takes way too long. 
On higher difficulties, that’s extremely annoying.

The bots themselves are alright. 
They kill a lot of enemies, share ammo, heal, and help you up, but they also get in the way a lot. 
If I aim down sights to snipe or shoot a group of zombies with an assault rifle, after two or three shots, a bot will randomly run back and forth in front of my shots, almost as if they’re doing it on purpose.

[h2] Overall, the game is fun for a while, but you have to be aware of a small player base and sometimes long waiting times to fill a lobby, unless you wanna play with friends or bots. 
There is no direct possibility to kick AFK players, and the annoying and unnecessary card perk system can kill the fun. 
I would not recommend buying this at full price, because it was never worth that.
However, if you get it as a key or on sale with the Annual Pass for around 9,99, it’s still a good purchase. [/h2]

I really gave this game a chance when it came out - I wanted it to be the successor to Left 4 Dead that it proclaimed to be. But ultimately there's too much going on in this game for it to work.

Let me explain.

What worked great about Left 4 Dead was that it allowed you to *breathe* - there are moments of quiet and fear that provide important contrast to the hordes, or allow you to hear the great sound design of the specials. This works great for a game about surviving a zombie apocalypse. Back 4 Blood discards all of this in favor of a constant stream of stimulation: gun COMPARISONS a la Borderlands, picking up GOLD to spend in SHOPS at each checkpoint, CARDS that change your game or playstyle, DECKS you build BEFORE you even play, CONSUMABLE cards you can APPLY before you play, RANDOM CARDS that appear on each map.

It's too much. None of these are bad ideas on their own, but together they're too much. I would have taken a Left 4 Dead where each character had a different ability / role - and no more. That alone would have been interesting. But the game loses the magic that the originals had because it bombards me with game mechanics that have no narrative basis in the world (why are there infinite supplies at each checkpoint? why do I need to pay money like it's a vending machine? why am I constantly stopping to compare guns while trying to move through a zombie-infested area? what even are CARDS?).

And the cherry on top? The characters just... won't shut up. If you're going to make the characters this chatty, at least make them entertaining/interesting (see Vermintide 2 for how it should be done).

Not even worth it if it's free. There are several other games that offer the same playstyle with much better experience. You either have to play with high ping, players failing on purpose or the dumbest bots I've ever seen in a co-op game. It's basically a point to point sprint, shooting mutated zombies with a few bosses. The only thing that makes this better than other similar games, is the custom modification. But gameplay in general, you can get WWZ or left for dead for less than half the price and much better value for money.

Too much working against this game:
========
--Bots--
========
Bot teammates are very infantile. They can alert snitches, hordes of enemies, and set off environmental hazards by randomly throwing molotovs at cars and explosive barrels. Regardless of what gun they hold, they barely do any damage unless it is on an easy difficulty (at which point the game is more of a walking simulator). 
- Bots cannot take nor use legendary rated gear
- Bots can take tool kits and then never use them
- When bots die and another bot has a Defib, they will not revive anyone unless you stand over the body and spam Q (ping) for about a minute at which point they will finally give in and use the item.
- Bots can hold on to medical accessories, but will rarely (if at all) use them, even if you are left with only a few points of health.
- If you die on "odd" terrain such as on a car; on stairs; on a barrel; on a fence; or any other terrain that isnt an easy flat ground, bots will not pick you up or use a defib. At best they will just run in circles around you.
- Bots can (and will) automatically take money, thus ruining the card "Heads, you lose" in which picking up copper can give you +5% damage for each copper pile or reset the effects you have gained thus far from the card.
- Bots are not "silent" even in silent missions; they will see an enemy and immediately shoot at it, alerting all of the enemies in the area, even if you are sniping from a distance with a suppressor
- For mission-critical items, a human player must carry them-- a bot will not pick them up (only exception being duffel bags which give a tiny cosmetic spray or profile icon when they carry it to the safe room)
- The bots have no sense of "cover" in that they will face and shoot in one direction that they choose, and you're left with looking behind you constantly for random enemies spawning from the ground.
- Bots can kill you if they throw a grenade at/near cars or explosives that you are near (and you cannot command them).
- The card "Down in Front" which disables friendly fire damage is essential as bots WILL run directly in front of you while you are firing (including constantly with LMGs) and get mowed down. They also seem to have some kind of coding that makes them run directly in front of any minigun that you set up and operate so they die faster.
- If a bot is near a bridge, they will fall off and die or be left hanging. If you are left hanging, they will "attempt" to pick you up like in L4D2 but in reality, they just run in front of you and let you die.

============
--Weapons--
============
Some of the gunplay is fun, but it feels like they are pushing for players to use either an LMG or shotgun. Every other gun comes nowhere near these two unless playing in a skilled 4-player co-op that values teamwork over screwing around.
You can also spend a large portion of a campaign upgrading one of your guns, only to have it outdone by a random gun lying around because it is a higher rarity (but same gun model and action).
The bow is just silly if you have the right deck for it (firing multiple arrows every second as though your traditional wooden bow is belt-fed with automatic firing).
The melee weapons, if you build your deck right, are insanely overpowered with the ability to heal on kill and grant yourself armor (although it can sometimes struggle with Ogres on the No Hope difficulty if earlygame.

===========
--Enemies--
===========
- All enemies can outrun you and attack while doing so. Getting hit significantly slows you down, meaning if your bot "allies" alert a horde or group of enemies, you will need to find a choke-point where enemies cannot spawn.
- Enemy spawns are very silly in a negative way, kind of like No More Room in Hell way back in the early days of Steam zombie games. You can clear a room and ensure it has no entry points, leave it for a second, and then turn around and find it full of enemies again. Similarly, if you block your field of view by looking at a wall or walking indoors (in an outside map), enemies can spawn infinitely, with a stupid amount spawning during hordes
- The "Tallboy"-style mutation is often the strongest, having incredibly high speed; the ability to grab you; an arm that takes out half your health in a single swing; and a very awkward weak point (its back shoulder where its oversized arm is, which it covers by holding behind its back). 
- Snitches (alerts the horde if not killed before it screams) can be set off by bots quietly (e.g. bots shoot at and kill the snitch, and a horde immediately follows but without the horde timer or scream). Additionally, theres sometimes a "Corruption Card" where even if you one-hit headshot a snitch from far away with a suppressed rifle, it will still alert the horde after it dies. 

The names for all the zombies are also ridiculous and annoying to memorize when bots call them out:
Hocker, Stalker, Stinger; Reeker, Retch, Exploder, Shredder; Bruiser, Crusher, Tallboy, Ripper; Sentinel, Wailer, Swarmer, Lobber; Snitcher; Sleeper; Breaker; Hag; Ogre; Abomination; Harbinger. For common zombies ("ridden"), you have: Common, armored, blighted, charred, volatile, festering, and armored soldiers (SWAT/military gear where your .50 cal rifle turns into a .22lr and headshots are useless until you break the armor).

=========
--Cards--
=========
The game uses a card-based upgrade system wherein after completing missions you gain supply points that can be spent on both permanent and burn cards. Burn cards are used one time only on the map that you select before starting the mission. If you select a burn card, you cannot unselect or change it; it auto-locks in, even if it was a misclick. If you try to save-scum it back (e.g. task kill before the mission starts), you just lose it.

The "permanent" cards are what you use before you start a mission. You can build a "Deck" with 15 cards, though, some of the cards are kind of necessary and waste slots (such as Down in Front to disable friendly fire while crouched so you dont slaughter all of your bot allies in a second of them walking in front of your barrel). There are a lot of varieties of card  types and special abilities they grant you, and it is painfully evident that card design was where the vast majority of the development of the game was focused on. So. Many. Cards. Yet, very few guns and basic QoL features (still no flashlights?)

There is far more that can be said about the wasted potential of this game such as the lack of map variety; the linear paths (some cars you can jump on, some you cant; some roofs will be invisible walls while some roofs will have a secret idol that gives an achievement). The game speaks for itself in these following points:
- No mod support. Check out the interview with Matt O'Driscoll (lead producer at Turtle Rock Studios) where the following was asked by Liana:

"So back in the day, I used to be a part of the Left 4 Dead modding community and uh, my BEST memories were learning coding and learning how to mess around with game files and stuff. Do you... is B4B going to facilitate the modding community at all, with the online element and all or... or is it gonna... purely be... contained game files?" 

Matt:
"Its contained at launch for sure. Yeah. We're not gonna have anything like that available then."
Liana says under her breath "...sad..."

- No proper flashlight support. From even when the game first launched, most if not all of the playerbase found that no buttons were assigned to a flashlight key in this VERY dark game. As it turns out, that is intentional-- the flashlight ONLY turns on in specific parts of certain maps where the devs have implemented a flashlight-friendly zone (kind of like a kill-zone for OOB, but intentional for flashlight "mechanics"). Theres much more, but I have hit the review character limit.

The name should not have been a declaration of war against Left 4 Dead. It’s no different than when reviewers would label games “Halo killers” back in the day and people were always up in arms when those games failed to live up to the hype. As some intelligent fellow steam users said in their reviews, this isn’t Left 4 Dead. It has many of the same mechanics, it does have the outer shell of L4D, but it’s ambitions are very different. 

Left 4 Dead already did what Turtle Rock and Valve wanted it to do. It exceeded all expectations. Back 4 Blood is not trying to usurp the throne (marketing aside), what it’s actually trying to do is offer a different take on the formula. With crazy amounts of replayability and build variety. The card system was an inspired idea. Though its very inclusion means scrolling through countless menus of cards and the filter system is severely lacking. Some people say the zombies (the Ridden) are lacking in artstyle or originality. To that I say, I genuinely don’t know what anyone expects out of these games anymore. You have many options within this sub-genre and most of them are licensed I.P.s. yet no one complains about the zombies in WWZ.

The ridden at the very least are distinct in how they appear to infect through gestation, rather than bites or blood transfer. Similar to Ridley Scott’s Aliens. When you kill them, you’ll see large worms wriggling around where they died. Instead of rescuing respawning teammates from closets, you’ll find them in pods stuck on walls, hanging there like the poor victims of Face Huggers from the Alien franchise. It is a small detail, but if you like lore as I do, you’ll appreciate the in-game fiction and how it explains why your poor teammate would actually still be alive.

Personally, I like the Ridden. The “corruption cards” which take the place of the L4D “director” choose which challenges players will face in every level and that lends to the previously mentioned replayability.

This game is at its best when you’re testing out a new build and feeling out the different playstyles.

It’s not Left 4 Dead, but that’s okay. It’s something else. If you like sci-fi and are not opposed to the modern zombie, there’s a lot to like here. It’s closer to something like “Slither” than Romero. It sorta feels Carpenter-esque. 

It’s wild how much Toxic Commando and this game have in common, considering Back 4 Blood came out in 2021 and Toxic Commando came out 2026 and the two were made by different studios. Of the two, I definitely prefer Back 4 Blood. The characters are actually memorable and the gameplay is far more replayable and enjoyable.

There are some standout finales in this game and the way missions are spaced out in “acts” versus single 4 or so chapter missions a la L4D, is cool, plus there is no penalty for leaving a mission as your progress is always saved at the start of each level. 

The hive mechanic is also pretty cool and gives further variety to the game. 

The only major downside to the game I haven’t mentioned (besides how confusing the menus can be) is that the multiplayer is dead. The bots are really solid. Except for how often they walk in front of your bullets. It is what it is. If you die, you can play as one of the bots and each character has individual lives that they can share with dead teammates. This game would be amazing with friends, but for the rest of us, at least the bots are better than those found in vanilla L4D.

Overall, a great underappreciated game. It's too bad we won't see a sequel or another game with this much ambition in its built-in build variety/replayability.
